A notary — most commonly referred to as a notary public — is a person officially appointed or licensed by a government to act as an impartial, trusted witness for important legal documents and transactions. Their core job is to verify that a signature on a document is genuine, that the person signing is who they claim to be, and that they signed willingly and with full awareness of what they were signing.
Why Notaries Exist

The fundamental reason notaries exist is fraud prevention.

Imagine you sign a property deed or a will today, but years later someone claims you never signed it — or that your signature was forged. A notary prevents this by standing there as an official, government-recognized witness at the exact moment of signing and creating a permanent official record of what happened.

When a notary verifies a document, that document is described as notarized. A notarized document carries far stronger legal weight than an ordinary unwitnessed one, because a trusted, government-authorized third party has officially confirmed its authenticity.
What a Notary Actually Does

A notary performs several specific official acts:

Witnessing a signature — This is the most common task. You appear before the notary, prove your identity (usually with a government-issued photo ID like a passport or driver's license), and sign your document in front of them. The notary then signs the document themselves and stamps it with their official seal. The whole process is called notarization.

Administering oaths and affirmations — A notary can legally swear you in before you make a sworn written statement (called an affidavit). Once you make a statement under oath before a notary, you are legally responsible for its truth. Lying in such a statement is a crime — the same as lying in court.

Certifying copies — A notary can officially confirm that a photocopy of an original document is a true and accurate copy of the original. This is useful when you must submit a copy of something important — like a birth certificate or a degree — to an institution, without handing over the irreplaceable original.

Acknowledging signatures — Sometimes you sign a document beforehand and then appear before the notary simply to confirm that the signature is yours and that you signed it freely, without pressure or force. This official confirmation is called an acknowledgment.
The Notary's Seal

Every notary has an official seal or stamp — a physical or digital mark applied to every document they notarize. This seal typically contains the notary's full name, their official title ("Notary Public"), the jurisdiction they are authorized in (such as a state or country), and often an expiration date for their authorization.

The seal is what makes a document officially notarized. Without it, the notarial act is incomplete and not legally valid.

Notaries also maintain a record book — called a journal or register — where they log every notarization they perform: the date, the document type, the signer's name, and the ID they presented. This creates a permanent, traceable record.
The Notary's Commission

A notary's official government authorization to perform notarizations is called their commission. In the United States, this is issued by a state government; in other countries, by the national or regional authority. Commissions typically have an expiration date — four years in many US states, for example — after which the notary must renew their authorization. A notary acting after their commission has expired is no longer legally authorized to notarize anything.
When You Need a Notary

You typically need a notary when signing documents with serious legal or financial consequences, such as:

  • Real estate transactions — buying or selling property, mortgage agreements
  • Wills and trusts — documents directing how your assets are handled after death
  • Power of attorney — documents authorizing someone else to make legal or financial decisions on your behalf
  • Affidavits — sworn written statements used in legal proceedings
  • Business contracts — certain high-stakes agreements between parties
  • Immigration and visa documents — many countries require notarization for applications
  • Loan agreements — particularly for large amounts
What a Notary Is NOT

This is an important distinction that many people miss.

In common law countries — such as the United States, the United Kingdom, India, Canada, and Australia — a notary is not a lawyer. They cannot give you legal advice, explain what a document's clauses mean, tell you whether you should sign something, or represent you in any legal matter. Their role is strictly and only about verifying identity, witnessing, and authenticating. If you need to understand a document's legal implications, you need a lawyer. A notary simply confirms that you signed — not what you were signing or whether you should have.

In civil law countries — much of continental Europe, Latin America, parts of Africa and Asia — a notary is a far more powerful and highly trained legal professional, often with qualifications similar to a lawyer. In these systems, a notary can draft legal documents, advise clients on legal matters, manage property transfers, and handle estate settlements. The role carries substantially more responsibility and expertise.
Remote (Online) Notarization

In recent years, many jurisdictions now permit remote online notarization (RON), where the entire notarization process happens over a secure video call rather than in person. You show your ID on camera, sign electronically, and the notary applies a digital seal. The legal outcome is the same as in-person notarization. This method has grown significantly in acceptance and is now legally recognized in a growing number of countries and US states.
Apostilles: Using Notarized Documents Internationally

If you need to use a notarized document in a foreign country, you may need an additional layer of certification called an apostille. An apostille is a certificate issued by a higher-level government authority (not the notary themselves) that verifies and authenticates the notary's own credentials — making the document legally recognized in other countries that are part of the Hague Apostille Convention. Think of it as an official "stamp of approval on the notary's stamp of approval," specifically for international use.
In Summary

A notary is an officially government-appointed witness whose job is to verify your identity, watch you sign important documents, administer oaths, and certify copies — all to prevent fraud and give legal documents official credibility and enforceability. The outcome of their work is a notarized document: one bearing an official seal, backed by a certified record, and carrying far stronger legal standing than an ordinary unwitnessed document. Their precise role varies by country — limited and strictly procedural in common law countries, broader and more legal in civil law countries — but their essential function everywhere is the same: to be a trustworthy, impartial, government-authorized witness that the law can rely on.
